newsitem.title: ITALY: Hard-left 'no' is serious wound - Italy's Veltroni.
newsitem.headline: Hard-left 'no' is serious wound - Italy's Veltroni.

text.p: Deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni said on Tuesday that a decision by the Communist Refoundation party to oppose sending an Italian-led security force to Albania was a serious wound to the governing alliance.
Veltroni called for a thorough review of the centre-left coalition's partnership with the hard-left party, which ensures the government's majority in the lower house of parliament.
Refoundation's 'no' to the mission "opens a serious wound that will require just as serious a review of relationships in the (parliamentary) majority," Veltroni told reporters.
He belongs to the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the biggest force in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government.
"What is certain is that we will undertake a serious political review that won't just concern the next 24 hours but the months of work ahead," Veltroni said.
Votes on deployment of the force are due in the Senate (upper house) later on Tuesday and the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) on Wednesday.
Centre-right backing for the deployment should assure the mission goes ahead but the Refoundation stance has raised questions about the longer-term cohesion of the government
Prodi pleaded again for united support for the Albania force on Tuesday, telling a businessmen's meeting in a speech that Italy's plans to lead it would test its seriousness in Europe.
"It is clear that Albania is deeply tied to our role in Europe," Prodi said. "This is also a way to be present in a single currency because our role as a major country will be recognised," he said.
The main opposition Freedom Alliance bloc was meeting on Tuesday to try to forge a common stance for the Albania votes.
The parties in the bloc agree that the force should go ahead but are split on whether they should also push for Prodi to acknowledge he has lost his parliamentary majority and resign.
Gianfranco Fini, leader of the hard right National Alliance party, and Rocco Buttiglione of the centrist CDU party, were taking a tough stance on the political approach.
"If you ask me, the normal thing is for the government to go to see the president and resign. If they don't want to do that let them tell us how they intend to govern," Buttiglione told reporters.
